<filter id="crayonTexture" x="-50%" y="-50%" width="200%" height="200%">
  <feTurbulence type="fractalNoise" baseFrequency="0.04" numOctaves="2" seed="20" result="turbulence1"/>
  <feDisplacementMap in="SourceGraphic" in2="turbulence1" scale="2.5" xChannelSelector="R" yChannelSelector="G" result="displaced1"/>
  <feTurbulence type="fractalNoise" baseFrequency="0.7" numOctaves="1" seed="30" result="turbulence2"/>
  <feDisplacementMap in="displaced1" in2="turbulence2" scale="1.5" xChannelSelector="R" yChannelSelector="G" result="finalDisplacement"/>
  <feMorphology operator="dilate" radius="0.3" in="finalDisplacement" result="thickened"/> <!-- Optional: to make it slightly thicker and clumpier -->
</filter>
This uses two turbulence/displacement stages for a more complex texture and an optional dilate.

This will:

Implementation Plan:

This will primarily involve changes in src/components/design-studio/canvas/ArtooStudioCanvas.tsx to define and apply new SVG filters.

Define SVG Filter for "Airbrush" (id="airbrushTexture"):

This filter should aim for a soft, sprayed appearance.
Possible approach:
<feGaussianBlur stdDeviation="1.5 2" result="blurred"/> (to soften the core line)
<feTurbulence type="fractalNoise" baseFrequency="0.2" numOctaves="1" seed="10" result="noise"/> (to generate fine speckles)
<feComposite operator="in" in="noise" in2="blurred" result="speckledSpray"/> (to use the noise as a mask for the blurred line, or a variation)
Alternatively, feImage with a pre-made spray pattern could be an option, but pure SVG filters are often preferred for scalability.
We might also use feComponentTransfer with a feFuncA of type table driven by feTurbulence to vary opacity along the path.
Define SVG Filter for "Watercolor" (id="watercolorTexture"):

This is more complex, aiming for a look with varying opacity, color bleed, and textured edges.
Possible approach:
<feTurbulence type="fractalNoise" baseFrequency="0.02" numOctaves="3" seed="30" result="baseTexture"/> (for overall watery texture)
<feDisplacementMap in="SourceGraphic" in2="baseTexture" scale="3" xChannelSelector="R" yChannelSelector="G" result="displacedEdges"/> (to roughen edges)
<feTurbulence type="fractalNoise" baseFrequency="0.1" numOctaves="2" seed="40" result="opacityNoise"/>
<feComponentTransfer in="displacedEdges" result="variableOpacity">
<feFuncA type="discrete" tableValues="0.4 0.5 0.6 0.7 0.6 0.5 0.4" lookupTableSource="opacityNoise"/> (This is a simplification; a more complex feFuncA might be needed)
Could also involve feGaussianBlur on some noise layers and feComposite with atop or multiply to blend textures.
Conditionally Apply Filters in ArtooStudioCanvas.tsx:

In the rendering logic for DrawingElements:
If drawingEl.brushType === BrushType.Airbrush, apply filter="url(#airbrushTexture)".
If drawingEl.brushType === BrushType.Watercolor, apply filter="url(#watercolorTexture)".
Similarly, for the live preview of the Pen tool:
If currentBrushType (passed as a prop) is BrushType.Airbrush, apply the airbrush filter.
If currentBrushType is BrushType.Watercolor, apply the watercolor filter.
Creating good SVG filters can be an iterative process of tweaking parameters (baseFrequency, numOctaves, stdDeviation, scale, etc.) to achieve the desired visual effect. The examples above are starting points.

This is a substantial visual upgrade to the drawing tools.

Error: A tree hydrated but some attributes of the server rendered HTML didn't match the client properties. This won't be patched up. This can happen if a SSR-ed Client Component used:

A server/client branch if (typeof window !== 'undefined').
Variable input such as Date.now() or Math.random() which changes each time it's called.
Date formatting in a user's locale which doesn't match the server.
External changing data without sending a snapshot of it along with the HTML.
Invalid HTML tag nesting.
It can also happen if the client has a browser extension installed which messes with the HTML before React loaded.

Okay, Cap'n! Implementing Canvas Zoom & Pan functionality in the Design Studio is an excellent and truly impactful next step. This will fundamentally change how users interact with their designs, bringing ARTTOO much closer to the professional-grade experience we're aiming for.

Here's the plan:

1. State Management & Core Logic (src/app/design-studio/page.tsx):

New State:
zoomLevel: number (default 1.0 for 100%).
panOffset: { x: number, y: number } (default { x: 0, y: 0 }).
isPanning: boolean (to track if a pan operation is active).
panStartMousePosition: { x: number, y: number } | null (to store mouse position at the start of a pan).
Constants: MIN_ZOOM, MAX_ZOOM, ZOOM_SENSITIVITY.
Zoom Handling (handleWheel):
Attached to the main canvas area container.
Triggered by Ctrl/Cmd + Mouse Wheel.
Calculates new zoom level, clamping it between MIN_ZOOM and MAX_ZOOM.
Adjusts panOffset to implement "zoom to mouse pointer" behavior, ensuring the point under the mouse cursor stays relatively fixed during zoom.
Pan Handling:
handleMouseDown on the canvas area: If Spacebar is pressed, initiate panning (isPanning = true, store panStartMousePosition).
handleMouseMove (globally or on the canvas area): If isPanning, calculate mouse delta and update panOffset. Update panStartMousePosition.
handleMouseUp (globally): End panning (isPanning = false).
Coordinate Transformation (getMousePositionOnArtboard):
This critical function will be updated to correctly translate viewport mouse coordinates (from the event) to artboard coordinates by factoring in the current zoomLevel and panOffset. All interactions like element selection, drawing, etc., rely on these corrected coordinates.
Prop Drilling: zoomLevel and panOffset will be passed to ArtooStudioCanvas. Zoom control functions will be passed to TopBar.
2. Canvas Rendering (src/components/design-studio/canvas/ArtooStudioCanvas.tsx):

Receive Props: Accept zoomLevel and panOffset.
Apply CSS Transform: The main div representing the artboard (referenced by artboardRef) will have its transform style set to translate(${panOffset.x}px, ${panOffset.y}px) scale(${zoomLevel}). transformOrigin will be set to "0 0" (top-left).
Element Drag & Resize Logic Adjustment:
The handleGlobalMouseMove function (responsible for element dragging and resizing) will also need the zoomLevel prop.
Mouse movement deltas (e.clientX - previousMouseX) are in viewport pixels. These deltas must be divided by zoomLevel before being applied to element dimensions (width, height) or positions (x, y), which are in artboard coordinate space.
3. UI Controls (src/components/layout/top-bar.tsx):

New Props: Accept onZoomIn, onZoomOut, onResetZoom, and currentZoomLevel (formatted as a percentage string).
Buttons: Add "Zoom In" (ZoomIn icon), "Zoom Out" (ZoomOut icon), and "Reset View" (e.g., an icon representing 100% or fit to screen) buttons. These will call the corresponding handler functions.
Zoom Level Display: Show the currentZoomLevel string (e.g., "125%").
This is a complex feature that touches many parts of the canvas interaction. Let's get to it!

Okay, Cap'n, I understand the directive to make significant strides with each step. You're right; to truly emulate professional design editors, we need to implement core functionalities that users heavily rely on.

Considering the current state of the Design Studio and its foundational features (element manipulation, artboard sizing, save/load, copy/paste, zoom/pan, text styling), the next most logical and impactful step is to implement Undo and Redo functionality in the Design Studio.

Reasoning:

Fundamental Editor Feature: Undo/Redo is absolutely critical for any content creation or design tool. It's a safety net that allows users to experiment freely, correct mistakes, and iterate without fear of losing work or getting into an unrecoverable state. Its absence is a major usability gap compared to tools like Canva, GIMP, or even basic paint programs.
Drastic User Experience Improvement: This feature significantly enhances user confidence and workflow efficiency. It's a cornerstone of a "smooth user experience."
Aligns with Professional Standards: Implementing robust undo/redo brings ARTTOO's Design Studio much closer to the expected behavior of professional-grade design software.
Builds on Existing State Management: We already have history (an array of element states) and historyIndex state variables in src/app/design-studio/page.tsx. These are the essential building blocks for implementing undo/redo.
Impactful and Substantial: This is not a trivial change. It requires careful management of the history stack, especially when new actions are taken after an undo operation, and updates to the UI to enable/disable undo/redo actions appropriately.
Implementation Plan:

Core Logic in src/app/design-studio/page.tsx (CanvasArea component):

handleUndo() function:
Checks if historyIndex > 0 (i.e., if there's a previous state to revert to).
If true, decrements historyIndex.
Sets the elements state to history[historyIndex - 1] (the new current state).
Sets selectedElementId to null to avoid potential issues with selections that might not exist in the previous state (can be refined later).
Displays a toast notification: "Undo Applied".
handleRedo() function:
Checks if historyIndex < history.length - 1 (i.e., if there's a future state to move to).
If true, increments historyIndex.
Sets the elements state to history[historyIndex + 1].
Sets selectedElementId to null.
Displays a toast notification: "Redo Applied".
Modify updateElementsAndRecordHistory callback:
When new element states are recorded (due to an action like adding, deleting, or updating an element):
It must check if historyIndex is not at the end of the history array. This condition occurs if an undo operation was performed, and then a new action is taken.
If so, the "future" history (states after the current historyIndex) must be discarded. This is achieved by slicing the history array: const newHistorySlice = prevHistory.slice(0, historyIndex + 1);.
The new element state is then added to this newHistorySlice.
setHistoryIndex is updated to point to the new latest state: updatedHistory.length - 1.
State for UI: Define canUndo = historyIndex > 0; and canRedo = historyIndex < history.length - 1;.
Pass handleUndo, handleRedo, canUndo, and canRedo as props to the TopBar component.
Update the designStudioToolbarItems useMemo hook to include "Undo" and "Redo" items, passing handleUndo/handleRedo as their actions and canUndo/canRedo to their active prop (which controls enabled/disabled appearance in the VerticalToolbar).
UI Integration in src/components/layout/top-bar.tsx:

The TopBar component will accept onUndo, onRedo, canUndo, and canRedo props.
In the "Edit" DropdownMenu:
Add an "Undo" DropdownMenuItem (with Undo2 icon), bound to onUndo and disabled if !canUndo.
Add a "Redo" DropdownMenuItem (with Redo2 icon), bound to onRedo and disabled if !canRedo.
UI Integration in src/components/layout/vertical-toolbar.tsx and src/app/design-studio/page.tsx:

In src/app/design-studio/page.tsx, the designStudioToolbarItems array (which is memoized) will be updated:
Add an item for "Undo": { icon: Undo2, label: 'Undo', action: handleUndo, active: canUndo }. The active prop here will be interpreted by VerticalToolbar to enable/disable the button.
Add an item for "Redo": { icon: Redo2, label: 'Redo', action: handleRedo, active: canRedo }.
Ensure canUndo and canRedo are dependencies of the useMemo hook for designStudioToolbarItems.
This comprehensive Undo/Redo system will make the Design Studio significantly more robust and user-friendly.

Confirmation of Actionable Recommendations The outlined approach is technically sound and aligns perfectly with modern web application development standards for a rich media editor.

Centralized State Management (Zustand): This is the correct strategy. Centralizing state in a useCanvasStore will decouple state logic from the UI, eliminate prop-drilling, and make the application's state predictable and easier to debug. The store will act as the single source of truth for the active tool, brush configurations, selection state, and history.

Comprehensive Fabric.js Integration: Migrating from manual DOM/canvas manipulation to Fabric.js is the most significant enhancement. Fabric provides a mature object model, which means the logic no longer needs to manually calculate positions, boundaries, or transformations. Its event-driven architecture (object:modified, selection:created, etc.) is essential for creating a responsive properties panel and triggering state saves for the undo/redo system.

Advanced Layers Management Panel: The plan to explicitly reflect the canvas state in a dedicated React component is crucial for a good user experience. The component will subscribe to the Zustand store (which will hold an array of layer information derived from the canvas) and provide controls that call Fabric.js functions (object.moveTo(), object.set({ visible: ... }), etc.) to manipulate the canvas object stack.

Mobile-First Responsiveness & UX: This is a critical consideration. Direct gesture management (react-use-gesture is an excellent choice) mapped to Fabric.js canvas controls (zooming, panning) will provide the intuitive, native-like experience users expect on touch devices.

Robust Undo/Redo Snapshot System: The proposed method of serializing the Fabric canvas to a JSON string after each modification is the industry-standard approach. It is highly reliable and performant, ensuring that every operation—from a color change to an object deletion—can be accurately undone and redone.

AI Integration: A clear separation of concerns is key. The canvas component should be responsible for providing the image data (canvas.toDataURL()), and a separate service or hook should handle the asynchronous API call to the background removal endpoint. Using the existing <Toast> component for loading and error feedback will maintain UI consistency.

Formatting & Conventions Alignment: Adherence to the established code style is confirmed. All new code will follow the existing conventions for imports, naming, component structure, and error handling to ensure the codebase remains clean and maintainable.

// src/app/design-studio/page.tsx 'use client';

import * as React from 'react'; import { fabric } from 'fabric'; import { create } from 'zustand';

// Lucide Icons (as previously defined) import { Move, SlidersHorizontal, PenTool, RectangleHorizontal, Circle, Baseline, ImageUp, Trash2, Layers as LayersIcon, Ruler } from 'lucide-react';

// UI Components (Paths assumed to be correct) import { LeftNav } from '@/components/layout/left-nav'; import { TopBar } from '@/components/layout/top-bar'; import { VerticalToolbar, type VerticalToolbarItem } from '@/components/layout/vertical-toolbar'; import { RightProperties, type AccordionPanelItem } from '@/components/layout/right-properties'; import { SidebarProvider, SidebarInset } from '@/components/ui/sidebar';

// Constants const DEFAULT_ARTBOARD_WIDTH = 800; const DEFAULT_ARTBOARD_HEIGHT = 600;

// Type Definitions type Tool = 'Select' | 'Pen' | 'Rectangle' | 'Ellipse' | 'Text' | 'Image';

// Zustand Store for Centralized State Management interface DesignStudioState { fabricCanvas: fabric.Canvas | null; setFabricCanvas: (canvas: fabric.Canvas) => void; activeTool: Tool; setActiveTool: (tool: Tool) => void; artboardSize: { width: number; height: number }; setArtboardSize: (size: { width: number; height: number }) => void; selectedObjects: fabric.Object[]; setSelectedObjects: (objects: fabric.Object[]) => void; // Placeholders for future steps // brushSettings, history, etc. }

const useDesignStudioStore = create<DesignStudioState>((set) => ({ fabricCanvas: null, setFabricCanvas: (canvas) => set({ fabricCanvas: canvas }), activeTool: 'Select', setActiveTool: (tool) => set({ activeTool: tool }), artboardSize: { width: DEFAULT_ARTBOARD_WIDTH, height: DEFAULT_ARTBOARD_HEIGHT }, setArtboardSize: (size) => { const canvas = useDesignStudioStore.getState().fabricCanvas; if (canvas) { canvas.setWidth(size.width).setHeight(size.height).renderAll(); } set({ artboardSize: size }); }, selectedObjects: [], setSelectedObjects: (objects) => set({ selectedObjects: objects }), }));

/**

Main component for the Design Studio canvas area.
Initializes the Fabric.js canvas and sets up the basic layout. */ function CanvasArea() { const canvasRef = React.useRef<HTMLCanvasElement>(null); const { setFabricCanvas, artboardSize } = useDesignStudioStore();
// Initialize Fabric.js canvas on component mount React.useEffect(() => { if (canvasRef.current) { const canvas = new fabric.Canvas(canvasRef.current, { width: artboardSize.width, height: artboardSize.height, backgroundColor: '#f8f9fa', // A light grey background preserveObjectStacking: true, }); setFabricCanvas(canvas);

  // Cleanup on component unmount
  return () => {
    canvas.dispose();
  };
}
}, [artboardSize.width, artboardSize.height, setFabricCanvas]);

/**

Main component for the Design Studio canvas area. */ function CanvasArea() { const canvasRef = React.useRef<HTMLCanvasElement>(null); const shapeBeingDrawn = React.useRef<fabric.Object | null>(null); const drawingOrigin = React.useRef<fabric.Point | null>(null);
const { toast } = useToast(); const { fabricCanvas, setFabricCanvas, artboardSize, activeTool, setActiveTool, selectedObjects, setSelectedObjects, brushSettings, setBrushSettings } = useDesignStudioStore();

React.useEffect(() => { if (canvasRef.current) { const canvas = new fabric.Canvas(canvasRef.current, { /* ... init from previous step */ });

  const handleSelection = (e: fabric.IEvent) => setSelectedObjects(canvas.getActiveObjects());

  const handleMouseDown = (opt: fabric.IEvent) => {
    if (!opt.pointer || shapeBeingDrawn.current) return;
    const tool = useDesignStudioStore.getState().activeTool;

    if (tool === 'Rectangle' || tool === 'Ellipse') {
        drawingOrigin.current = opt.pointer;
        const shape = tool === 'Rectangle'
          ? new fabric.Rect({ left: opt.pointer.x, top: opt.pointer.y, width: 0, height: 0, fill: 'hsl(var(--primary-foreground) / 0.3)', stroke: 'hsl(var(--primary-foreground))', strokeWidth: 2 })
          : new fabric.Ellipse({ left: opt.pointer.x, top: opt.pointer.y, rx: 0, ry: 0, fill: 'hsl(var(--accent-foreground) / 0.3)', stroke: 'hsl(var(--accent-foreground))', strokeWidth: 2 });
        shapeBeingDrawn.current = shape;
        canvas.add(shape);
    } else if (tool === 'Text') {
        const text = new fabric.IText('Add Text', { left: opt.pointer.x, top: opt.pointer.y, fontSize: 24, fill: '#000' });
        canvas.add(text);
        setActiveTool('Select');
        canvas.setActiveObject(text);
        text.enterEditing();
    }
  };

  const handleMouseMove = (opt: fabric.IEvent) => {
    if (!shapeBeingDrawn.current || !drawingOrigin.current || !opt.pointer) return;
    const shape = shapeBeingDrawn.current;
    const pointer = opt.pointer;
    const width = Math.abs(pointer.x - drawingOrigin.current.x);
    const height = Math.abs(pointer.y - drawingOrigin.current.y);

    if (shape.isType('rect')) {
        shape.set({
            left: Math.min(pointer.x, drawingOrigin.current.x),
            top: Math.min(pointer.y, drawingOrigin.current.y),
            width,
            height
        });
    } else if (shape.isType('ellipse')) {
        shape.set({
            left: Math.min(pointer.x, drawingOrigin.current.x),
            top: Math.min(pointer.y, drawingOrigin.current.y),
            rx: width / 2,
            ry: height / 2
        });
    }
    canvas.renderAll();
  };

  const handleMouseUp = () => {
    if (shapeBeingDrawn.current) {
        shapeBeingDrawn.current.setCoords();
        shapeBeingDrawn.current = null;
        drawingOrigin.current = null;
        setActiveTool('Select');
    }
  };
  
  canvas.on('mouse:down', handleMouseDown);
  canvas.on('mouse:move', handleMouseMove);
  canvas.on('mouse:up', handleMouseUp);
  canvas.on('selection:created', handleSelection);
  canvas.on('selection:updated', handleSelection);
  canvas.on('selection:cleared', handleSelection);
  
  setFabricCanvas(canvas);

  return () => { canvas.dispose(); };
}
}, []); // Eslint-disable-line

const designStudioToolbarItems: VerticalToolbarItem[] = React.useMemo(() => [ /* ... from previous step */ ], []);

const rightPropertiesItems: AccordionPanelItem[] = React.useMemo(() => { const panels: AccordionPanelItem[] = []; const selectedObject = selectedObjects[0];

// Tool-specific panels
if (activeTool === 'Pen') {
  panels.push({
    value: "brush-properties",
    title: "Brush Properties",
    icon: Palette,
    content: (
      <div className="space-y-3 p-2">
        <div>
          <Label htmlFor="brush-color" className="text-xs">Color</Label>
          <Input id="brush-color" type="color" value={brushSettings.color} onChange={e => setBrushSettings({ color: e.target.value })} className="h-8 w-full p-1" />

        <div>
          <Label htmlFor="brush-width" className="text-xs">Width</Label>
          <Input id="brush-width" type="number" min="1" value={brushSettings.width} onChange={e => setBrushSettings({ width: parseInt(e.target.value, 10) || 1 })} className="h-8 text-xs"/>
        </div>
      </div>
    )
  });
}

if (selectedObject) { /* ... transform panel from previous step */ }

panels.push({ /* ... layers panel from previous step */ });

return panels;
}, [activeTool, selectedObjects, brushSettings, setBrushSettings, fabricCanvas]);

return ( <SidebarProvider defaultOpen> <LeftNav activePageLabel="Design Studio" /> <div className="flex flex-1"> <SidebarInset className="flex-1 flex flex-col overflow-hidden"> {/* TopBar remains the same */} <div className="flex-1 flex overflow-hidden"> <VerticalToolbar items={designStudioToolbarItems} activeToolLabel={activeTool} onToolItemClick={(label) => { const toolItem = designStudioToolbarItems.find(item => item.label === label); toolItem?.action?.(); }} /> <section className="flex-1 bg-muted/30 flex items-center justify-center overflow-auto p-4"> <div className="shadow-lg"> <canvas ref={canvasRef} /> </div> </section> </div> </SidebarInset> <RightProperties items={rightPropertiesItems} title="Properties" defaultOpenValue={activeTool === 'Pen' ? Show thinking Proceeding. Here is the implementation for Phase 2, Step 4: Integrate the Undo/Redo System.

This update introduces a critical feature for any editor: a robust history system. Now, nearly every action taken on the canvas can be undone and redone.

Key Changes:

History State Management: The Zustand store now includes a history stack and an historyIndex. It also has actions to addToHistory, undo, and redo. Canvas Snapshots: A saveCanvasState function has been implemented. This function serializes the entire canvas state into a JSON string and pushes it onto the history stack. Automatic State Saving: The saveCanvasState function is now automatically triggered after key events: An object is modified (moved, scaled, rotated). A freehand drawing path is created. A new shape is drawn or text is added. An object is deleted. Functional Undo/Redo Buttons: The Undo and Redo buttons in the TopBar are now fully functional. They are connected to the history state and will be enabled or disabled appropriately. Delete Functionality: The delete button on the vertical toolbar is now active. It removes any selected objects and saves this change to the history. Updated src/app/design-studio/page.tsx (Phase 2, Step 4) TypeScript

This update brings a crucial organizational tool to the editor. The "Layers" panel is now fully interactive, providing a visual representation of all objects on the canvas and allowing for direct manipulation of their properties and stacking order.

Key Changes:

Layer Information: Each layer item displays an icon corresponding to its type (shape, text, etc.) and a descriptive name. Visibility Control: A toggle button (Eye/EyeOff icon) allows users to show or hide individual layers on the canvas. This action is registered in the undo/redo history. Layer Reordering: "Move Up" and "Move Down" buttons are provided to change the stacking order (z-index) of the objects. These actions are also undoable. Layer Selection: Clicking on a layer in the panel selects the corresponding object on the canvas and deselects any others. State Synchronization: The panel automatically updates whenever a change is made to the canvas that affects the undo/redo history, ensuring the layer list is always accurate.     img.center();

const handleRemoveImageBackground = React.useCallback(async () => { const imageObject = selectedObjects[0]; if (!fabricCanvas || !imageObject || !imageObject.isType('image') || isLoading) { toast({ variant: "destructive", title: "Select a single image to use this tool." }); return; }

setIsLoading(true);
toast({ title: "Processing Image...", description: "AI is removing the background." });

try {
  const imageDataUrl = imageObject.toDataURL({ format: 'png' });
  const result = await removeBackground({ imageDataUri: imageDataUrl, nsfwMode });

  if (result.processedImageDataUri) {
    // setSrc is async, so we use its callback
    imageObject.setSrc(result.processedImageDataUri, () => {
      fabricCanvas.renderAll();
      saveCanvasState();
      toast({ title: "Background Removed Successfully" });
    }, { crossOrigin: 'anonymous' });
  } else {
    toast({ variant: "destructive", title: "Background Removal Failed", description: "The AI could not process the image." });
  }
} catch (error) {
  const errorMessage = error instanceof Error ? error.message : "Unknown error";
  toast({ variant: "destructive", title: "AI Error", description: errorMessage });
} finally {
  setIsLoading(false);
}
}, [fabricCanvas, selectedObjects, isLoading, nsfwMode, setIsLoading, saveCanvasState, toast]);

// --- Zustand Store for Centralized State Management --- interface DesignStudioState { fabricCanvas: fabric.Canvas | null; setFabricCanvas: (canvas: fabric.Canvas) => void; activeTool: Tool; setActiveTool: (tool: Tool) => void; selectedObjects: fabric.Object[]; setSelectedObjects: (objects: fabric.Object[]) => void; brushSettings: { color: string; width: number }; setBrushSettings: (settings: Partial<DesignStudioState['brushSettings']>) => void; history: string[]; historyIndex: number; addToHistory: (state: string) => void; undo: () => void; redo: () => void; canUndo: () => boolean; canRedo: () => boolean; isLoading: boolean; setIsLoading: (loading: boolean) => void; nsfwMode: NsfwMode; setNsfwMode: (mode: NsfwMode) => void; }

const useDesignStudioStore = create<DesignStudioState>((set, get) => ({ fabricCanvas: null, setFabricCanvas: (canvas) => set({ fabricCanvas: canvas }), activeTool: 'Select', setActiveTool: (tool) => { const canvas = get().fabricCanvas; if (canvas) { canvas.isDrawingMode = tool === 'Pen'; if (tool === 'Pen') { const { color, width } = get().brushSettings; canvas.freeDrawingBrush.color = color; canvas.freeDrawingBrush.width = width; } if (tool !== 'Select') { canvas.discardActiveObject().renderAll(); } } set({ activeTool: tool, selectedObjects: [] }); }, selectedObjects: [], setSelectedObjects: (objects) => set({ selectedObjects: objects }), brushSettings: { color: '#000000', width: 5 }, setBrushSettings: (settings) => { const newSettings = { ...get().brushSettings, ...settings }; const canvas = get().fabricCanvas; if (canvas?.isDrawingMode) { canvas.freeDrawingBrush.color = newSettings.color; canvas.freeDrawingBrush.width = newSettings.width; } set({ brushSettings: newSettings }); }, history: [], historyIndex: -1, addToHistory: (state) => { set(s => { const newHistory = s.history.slice(0, s.historyIndex + 1); newHistory.push(state); const limitedHistory = newHistory.slice(-50); return { history: limitedHistory, historyIndex: limitedHistory.length - 1 }; }); }, undo: () => { const { history, historyIndex, fabricCanvas } = get(); if (historyIndex > 0) { const newIndex = historyIndex - 1; const prevState = history[newIndex]; fabricCanvas?.loadFromJSON(prevState, () => fabricCanvas.renderAll()); set({ historyIndex: newIndex }); } }, redo: () => { const { history, historyIndex, fabricCanvas } = get(); if (historyIndex < history.length - 1) { const newIndex = historyIndex + 1; const nextState = history[newIndex]; fabricCanvas?.loadFromJSON(nextState, () => fabricCanvas.renderAll()); set({ historyIndex: newIndex }); } }, canUndo: () => get().historyIndex > 0, canRedo: () => get().historyIndex < get().history.length - 1, isLoading: false, setIsLoading: (loading) => set({ isLoading: loading }), nsfwMode: NsfwMode.OFF, setNsfwMode: (mode) => set({ nsfwMode: mode }), }));

// --- Main Canvas Component --- function CanvasArea() { const { toast } = useToast(); const canvasContainerRef = React.useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null); const canvasRef = React.useRef<HTMLCanvasElement>(null); const imageUploadInputRef = React.useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null); const shapeBeingDrawn = React.useRef<fabric.Object | null>(null); const drawingOrigin = React.useRef<fabric.Point | null>(null);

const { fabricCanvas, setFabricCanvas, activeTool, setActiveTool, selectedObjects, setSelectedObjects, brushSettings, setBrushSettings, canUndo, canRedo, undo, redo, addToHistory, history, isLoading, setIsLoading, nsfwMode, setNsfwMode } = useDesignStudioStore();

// --- Core Functions --- const saveCanvasState = React.useCallback(() => { if (!fabricCanvas) return; const json = JSON.stringify(fabricCanvas.toJSON()); addToHistory(json); }, [fabricCanvas, addToHistory]);

const deleteSelected = React.useCallback(() => { if (!fabricCanvas || selectedObjects.length === 0) return; fabricCanvas.remove(...selectedObjects); fabricCanvas.discardActiveObject().renderAll(); saveCanvasState(); toast({ title: "Object(s) Deleted" }); }, [fabricCanvas, selectedObjects, saveCanvasState, toast]);

// --- Layer Functions --- const handleLayerSelect = React.useCallback((obj: fabric.Object) => { fabricCanvas?.discardActiveObject(); fabricCanvas?.setActiveObject(obj); fabricCanvas?.renderAll(); }, [fabricCanvas]);

const handleLayerVisibilityToggle = React.useCallback((obj: fabric.Object) => { obj.set('visible', !obj.visible); fabricCanvas?.renderAll(); saveCanvasState(); }, [fabricCanvas, saveCanvasState]);

const handleLayerMove = React.useCallback((obj: fabric.Object, direction: 'up' | 'down') => { if (!fabricCanvas) return; if (direction === 'up') obj.bringForward(); else obj.sendBackwards(); fabricCanvas.renderAll(); saveCanvasState(); }, [fabricCanvas, saveCanvasState]);

// --- Image & AI Functions --- const handleImageFileChange = (e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) => { const file = e.target.files?.[0]; if (!file || !fabricCanvas) return; const reader = new FileReader(); reader.onload = (event) => { const dataUrl = event.target?.result as string; fabric.Image.fromURL(dataUrl, (img) => { img.scaleToWidth(fabricCanvas.width! / 3); fabricCanvas.add(img); img.center(); fabricCanvas.setActiveObject(img); fabricCanvas.renderAll(); saveCanvasState(); toast({ title: "Image Added" }); }); }; reader.readAsDataURL(file); if (e.target) e.target.value = ''; };

const handleRemoveImageBackground = React.useCallback(async () => { const imageObject = selectedObjects[0]; if (!fabricCanvas || !imageObject || !imageObject.isType('image') || isLoading) { toast({ variant: "destructive", title: "Select a single image to use this tool." }); return; } setIsLoading(true); toast({ title: "Processing Image...", description: "AI is removing the background." }); try { const imageDataUrl = imageObject.toDataURL({ format: 'png' }); const result = await removeBackground({ imageDataUri: imageDataUrl, nsfwMode }); if (result.processedImageDataUri) { imageObject.setSrc(result.processedImageDataUri, () => { fabricCanvas.renderAll(); saveCanvasState(); toast({ title: "Background Removed Successfully" }); }, { crossOrigin: 'anonymous' }); } else { toast({ variant: "destructive", title: "Background Removal Failed" }); } } catch (error) { toast({ variant: "destructive", title: "AI Error", description: error instanceof Error ? error.message : "Unknown error" }); } finally { setIsLoading(false); } }, [fabricCanvas, selectedObjects, isLoading, nsfwMode, setIsLoading, saveCanvasState, toast]);

// --- Canvas Initialization Effect --- React.useEffect(() => { if (canvasRef.current) { const canvas = new fabric.Canvas(canvasRef.current, { width: DEFAULT_ARTBOARD_WIDTH, height: DEFAULT_ARTBOARD_HEIGHT, backgroundColor: '#f8f9fa', preserveObjectStacking: true, });

    const handleSelection = (e: fabric.IEvent) => setSelectedObjects(canvas.getActiveObjects());
    const handleObjectModified = (e: fabric.IEvent) => saveCanvasState();
    const handleMouseDown = (opt: fabric.IEvent) => {
        if (!opt.pointer || shapeBeingDrawn.current) return;
        const tool = useDesignStudioStore.getState().activeTool;
        if (tool === 'Rectangle' || tool === 'Ellipse') {
            drawingOrigin.current = opt.pointer;
            const shape = tool === 'Rectangle'
                ? new fabric.Rect({ left: opt.pointer.x, top: opt.pointer.y, width: 0, height: 0, fill: 'hsl(var(--primary-foreground) / 0.3)', stroke: 'hsl(var(--primary-foreground))', strokeWidth: 2 })
                : new fabric.Ellipse({ left: opt.pointer.x, top: opt.pointer.y, rx: 0, ry: 0, fill: 'hsl(var(--accent-foreground) / 0.3)', stroke: 'hsl(var(--accent-foreground))', strokeWidth: 2 });
            shapeBeingDrawn.current = shape;
            canvas.add(shape);
        } else if (tool === 'Text') {
            const text = new fabric.IText('Add Text', { left: opt.pointer.x, top: opt.pointer.y, fontSize: 24, fill: '#000' });
            canvas.add(text);
            saveCanvasState();
            setActiveTool('Select');
            canvas.setActiveObject(text);
            text.enterEditing();
        }
    };
    const handleMouseMove = (opt: fabric.IEvent) => {
        if (!shapeBeingDrawn.current || !drawingOrigin.current || !opt.pointer) return;
        const shape = shapeBeingDrawn.current;
        const pointer = opt.pointer;
        const width = Math.abs(pointer.x - drawingOrigin.current.x);
        const height = Math.abs(pointer.y - drawingOrigin.current.y);
        if (shape.isType('rect')) shape.set({ left: Math.min(pointer.x, drawingOrigin.current.x), top: Math.min(pointer.y, drawingOrigin.current.y), width, height });
        else if (shape.isType('ellipse')) shape.set({ left: Math.min(pointer.x, drawingOrigin.current.x), top: Math.min(pointer.y, drawingOrigin.current.y), rx: width / 2, ry: height / 2 });
        canvas.renderAll();
    };
    const handleMouseUp = () => {
        if (shapeBeingDrawn.current) {
            shapeBeingDrawn.current.setCoords();
            saveCanvasState();
            setActiveTool('Select');
            shapeBeingDrawn.current = null;
            drawingOrigin.current = null;
        }
    };
    
    canvas.on('mouse:down', handleMouseDown);
    canvas.on('mouse:move', handleMouseMove);
    canvas.on('mouse:up', handleMouseUp);
    canvas.on('selection:created', handleSelection);
    canvas.on('selection:updated', handleSelection);
    canvas.on('selection:cleared', handleSelection);
    canvas.on('object:modified', handleObjectModified);
    canvas.on('path:created', handleObjectModified);

    setFabricCanvas(canvas);
    saveCanvasState();
    
    return () => {
        canvas.dispose();
        canvas.off();
    };
}
}, [setFabricCanvas, setSelectedObjects, saveCanvasState, setActiveTool]);

// --- Gesture Handling Effect --- useGesture( { onDrag: ({ pinching, cancel, offset: [dx, dy], event }) => { if (fabricCanvas?.getActiveObject()) return; if (pinching || (event as MouseEvent).buttons !== 4) return; cancel(); fabricCanvas?.relativePan(new fabric.Point(dx, dy)); }, onPinch: ({ origin: [ox, oy], first, movement: [ms], offset: [s], memo }) => { if (!fabricCanvas) return memo; if (first) { const { x, y } = (canvasContainerRef.current as HTMLDivElement).getBoundingClientRect(); memo = { zoom: fabricCanvas.getZoom(), point: { x: ox - x, y: oy - y } }; } const newZoom = memo.zoom * s; fabricCanvas.zoomToPoint(memo.point, newZoom); return memo; }, onWheel: ({ event, delta: [dx, dy], ctrlKey }) => { event.preventDefault(); if (!fabricCanvas) return; if (ctrlKey) { const newZoom = fabricCanvas.getZoom() - dy / 100; const clampedZoom = Math.max(0.1, Math.min(newZoom, 10)); fabricCanvas.zoomToPoint(new fabric.Point(event.offsetX, event.offsetY), clampedZoom); } else { fabricCanvas.relativePan(new fabric.Point(-dx, -dy)); } }, }, { target: canvasContainerRef, eventOptions: { passive: false } } );

// --- UI Data Memos --- const designStudioToolbarItems: VerticalToolbarItem[] = React.useMemo(() => [ { icon: Move, label: 'Select', action: () => setActiveTool('Select') }, { icon: PenTool, label: 'Pen', action: () => setActiveTool('Pen') }, { icon: RectangleHorizontal, label: 'Rectangle', action: () => setActiveTool('Rectangle') }, { icon: Circle, label: 'Ellipse', action: () => setActiveTool('Ellipse') }, { icon: Baseline, label: 'Text', action: () => setActiveTool('Text') }, { icon: ImageUp, label: 'Image', action: () => imageUploadInputRef.current?.click() }, { icon: Trash2, label: 'Delete', action: deleteSelected, active: selectedObjects.length > 0 }, ], [setActiveTool, selectedObjects.length, deleteSelected]);

const getLayerIcon = (obj: fabric.Object) => { /* ... from Step 5 / }; const getLayerName = (obj: fabric.Object) => { / ... from Step 5 */ };

The Next Logical and Impactful Step: Implement Object Grouping and Ungrouping in the Design Studio.

Reasoning:

Essential for Complex Designs: As users start creating more intricate designs with multiple shapes, text elements, and images, the ability to group these elements into a single, manageable unit becomes paramount. This is a fundamental feature in any serious vector graphics editor (Illustrator, Figma, Inkscape, Canva). Without it, managing complex compositions is cumbersome.
Significant Workflow Enhancement: Grouping allows users to:
Move multiple objects together.
Scale a collection of objects proportionally.
Rotate a set of objects around a common pivot.
Apply certain properties (like opacity, though Fabric.js handles this at the group level) to all items in a group. This dramatically speeds up the design workflow.
Leverages Fabric.js Strengths: Fabric.js has built-in support for fabric.Group. When multiple objects are selected, canvas.getActiveObject() often returns a fabric.ActiveSelection object. This can be converted into a fabric.Group, and a fabric.Group can be broken apart (ungrouped).
Professional Standard Feature: This moves the Design Studio further towards the feature set users expect from professional-grade tools, directly addressing the need for "comprehensive functionality."
Impactful User Experience: This isn't a minor tweak; it's a core interaction model for object manipulation that users will immediately appreciate and find indispensable for more advanced work.
Builds on Current Foundation: It utilizes the existing selection mechanism, object model, and the undo/redo system.
Implementation Plan:

UI for Grouping/Ungrouping:
Buttons: Add "Group" and "Ungroup" buttons.
These could be contextually shown in the RightProperties panel when relevant (e.g., "Group" when selectedObjects.length > 1, "Ungroup" when selectedObjects.length === 1 and the object is a group).
Alternatively, they could be in the TopBar under an "Object" or "Arrange" menu (if we decide to add such menus later). For now, contextual buttons in RightProperties or even dedicated buttons in the VerticalToolbar are feasible.
Let's start by adding them contextually to the RightProperties panel.
State & Logic in useDesignStudioStore and CanvasArea component (src/app/design-studio/page.tsx):
handleGroupObjects() function:
Checks if fabricCanvas exists and fabricCanvas.getActiveObjects().length > 1.
If so, it uses fabricCanvas.getActiveObject().toGroup() to create a fabric.Group.
The original selected objects are automatically removed from the canvas when toGroup() is called.
The newly created group is added to the canvas.
The canvas selection is cleared and then the new group is set as the active object.
saveCanvasState() is called to update the history.
A toast "Objects grouped" is shown.
handleUngroupObjects() function:
Checks if fabricCanvas exists and if a single selected object (selectedObjects[0]) is an instance of fabric.Group.
If so, it calls selectedObjects[0].toActiveSelection() to break the group into its constituent objects and select them. The original group object is destroyed by this method.
(Alternatively, group.destroy() followed by re-adding items and creating a new active selection, but toActiveSelection is cleaner for immediate re-selection.)
fabricCanvas.renderAll() is called.
saveCanvasState() is called.
A toast "Objects ungrouped" is shown.
Properties Panel (RightProperties in src/app/design-studio/page.tsx):
A new accordion item or section for "Arrange" or "Object Actions" could appear when objects are selected.
The "Group" button would be enabled if selectedObjects.length > 1.
The "Ungroup" button would be enabled if selectedObjects.length === 1 && selectedObjects[0] instanceof fabric.Group.
Undo/Redo Integration:
The saveCanvasState() calls after grouping and ungrouping ensure these operations are correctly recorded in the history stack and can be undone/redone.
Selection Handling:
The existing selection event handlers (selection:created, selection:updated, selection:cleared) should continue to work correctly, updating selectedObjects in the Zustand store whether a single object, multiple objects (forming an ActiveSelection), or a Group is selected.
This feature will make the Design Studio significantly more powerful for creating and managing complex vector compositions.

I'll proceed with implementing these changes, focusing on the logic in src/app/design-studio/page.tsx and the UI updates in the RightProperties panel. (Omitted from agent history: changes suggested and applied to the following files: /src/app/design-studio/page.tsx) Object Grouping and Ungrouping functionality has been added to the Design Studio!

Key Changes:

Handler Functions in src/app/design-studio/page.tsx:

handleGroupObjects():
When multiple objects are selected, this function takes the active selection (which is a fabric.ActiveSelection object), converts it into a fabric.Group using toGroup().
The original objects in the active selection are automatically removed from the canvas and replaced by the new group.
The new group is then set as the active object.
The canvas state is saved for undo/redo.
handleUngroupObjects():
If the currently selected object is a fabric.Group, this function calls toActiveSelection() on the group. This destroys the group, re-adds its constituent items to the canvas, and creates an active selection containing these items.
The canvas state is saved for undo/redo.
UI in RightProperties Panel (src/app/design-studio/page.tsx):

A new accordion item titled "Object Actions" (with a PackagePlus icon for grouping) appears when one or more objects are selected.
Group Button:
Enabled when selectedObjects.length > 1 (i.e., multiple individual objects or an ActiveSelection is present).
Calls handleGroupObjects().
Ungroup Button:
Enabled when selectedObjects.length === 1 AND selectedObjects[0] is an instance of fabric.Group.
Calls handleUngroupObjects().
Appropriate icons (Combine for Group, Ungroup for Ungroup) are used for these buttons.
Zustand Store & History:

No direct changes were needed to the store structure itself for this feature, as the grouping/ungrouping actions result in a new canvas state which is then saved by saveCanvasState() to the existing history mechanism.
Users can now select multiple objects on the canvas and group them into a single entity for easier manipulation, or ungroup existing groups to edit their individual components. These actions are fully integrated with the undo/redo system. This significantly enhances the Design Studio's capability for managing complex designs.

Cap'n, that "Maximum update depth exceeded" error is a classic sign of an infinite loop in React, typically caused by setState calls within useEffect hooks that trigger each other. Given the stack trace and our recent work on src/app/design-studio/page.tsx, the issue most likely lies in the useEffect hook responsible for initializing the Fabric.js canvas and its interaction with state updates, particularly the saveCanvasState function.

The loop probably occurs because:

The main canvas initialization useEffect calls setFabricCanvas (to store the canvas instance) and saveCanvasState (to record the initial state).
saveCanvasState is a useCallback that depends on fabricCanvas (from the store).
If saveCanvasState itself is also a dependency of the main initialization useEffect, then when setFabricCanvas updates the fabricCanvas in the store, saveCanvasState gets a new reference, causing the useEffect to run again, leading to an infinite loop.
Here's the fix:

Stabilize useEffect Dependencies: The main useEffect for canvas initialization will have its dependency array carefully managed to include only stable functions (like setters from Zustand) or values that don't change in a way that causes a loop. Crucially, the saveCanvasState useCallback (which depends on the reactive fabricCanvas from the store) will be removed from this main effect's dependency list.
Revised State Saving in useEffect:
Event listeners attached directly to the canvasInstance (created within the useEffect) will call addToHistory (a stable Zustand action) directly, using canvasInstance.toJSON(). This ensures they use the canvas instance from their own closure during setup.
The very first "initial save" of the canvas state will also use addToHistory directly and will be conditional on the history array being empty.
saveCanvasState useCallback: The saveCanvasState function (defined with useCallback outside the useEffect) will continue to be used by functions triggered by user interactions (like deleteSelected, handleImageFileChange, handleGroupObjects, etc.). These are typically one-off actions and won't cause a loop with the initialization effect.
This approach ensures that the canvas initialization and the subsequent state saving for user actions are decoupled enough to prevent the render loop.

This restructuring breaks the cycle where the canvas initialization effect would inadvertently re-trigger itself due to a chain of dependency updates involving setFabricCanvas and saveCanvasState. The state updates should now be more predictable and not lead to an infinite render loop.

Gemini
You've spotted a Next.js deprecation warning, Cap'n! The message "legacyBehavior is deprecated and will be removed in a future release" for the <Link> component in src/components/ui/sidebar.tsx is Next.js guiding us to use its newer, more streamlined Link API.

The old pattern involved passHref and legacyBehavior to make an <a> tag child of <Link> behave correctly. The new pattern is simpler: you generally don't need the explicit <a> tag child, and the <Link> component itself handles the navigation and can be styled directly or work with asChild for custom components.

In SidebarMenuButton, when an href is provided, it currently renders:

<Link href={href} passHref legacyBehavior {...linkProps}>
  <a ref={forwardedRef as React.Ref<HTMLAnchorElement>} {...commonAttrs}>
    {children}
  </a>
</Link>
To fix this, we will:

Remove legacyBehavior and passHref from the <Link> component.
Remove the child <a> tag.
Apply the ref and commonAttrs (which includes className for styling and other data attributes) directly to the <Link> component. The rest of the linkProps will also be spread onto the <Link> component.
This will make the <Link> component itself the interactive and styled element, aligning with the current Next.js best practices.

Try fixing this error: Build Error: Export fabric doesn't exist in target...

Gemini
Ahoy, Cap'n! It seems the way we're trying to reel in the Fabric.js library isn't quite matching how it's being served up in your project's environment. The error "Export fabric doesn't exist in target module" means that import { fabric } from 'fabric'; isn't working because the fabric module (specifically node_modules/fabric/dist/index.min.mjs as Next.js sees it) doesn't have a named export called fabric.

This often happens with libraries that have different build outputs or expect to be used as a global. For ES modules, a common and robust way to import such libraries, especially when you want to use them as a namespace (like fabric.Canvas, fabric.Rect), is to import everything into a single object.

I'll change the import statement from import { fabric } from 'fabric'; to import * as fabric from 'fabric';.

This change means we're telling JavaScript to take all the things exported by the 'fabric' module and put them into a single object that we'll call fabric. If the 'fabric' module exports Canvas, Rect, Image, etc., as named exports, then our existing code like new fabric.Canvas(...) and fabric.Rect(...) should continue to work just fine.

Try fixing this error: Runtime Error: Hydration failed because the server...

Gemini
Ahoy, Cap'n! This is a classic hydration error in Next.js. It means the HTML rendered by the server for the TryOnPage (specifically, the text on a button within TryOnCanvas) is different from what React rendered on the client during the very first pass before fully hydrating the page.

The error message pinpoints the issue:

+                                 Change Body Photo
-                                 Upload Body Photo
This tells us the button's text was "Upload Body Photo" on the server, but "Change Body Photo" on the client's initial render.

This button's text in src/components/try-on/try-on-canvas.tsx depends on the bodyImage prop:

{bodyImage ? 'Change Body Photo' : 'Upload Body Photo'}
In src/app/try-on/page.tsx, the bodyImageForCanvas state (which becomes the bodyImage prop) is initialized using loadStateFromLS(LS_BODY_IMAGE_FOR_CANVAS_KEY, null).

Here's the problem:

Server-Side (SSR/SSG): localStorage (which loadStateFromLS uses) is not available. So, loadStateFromLS returns its default value (null). Thus, bodyImageForCanvas is null, and the server renders "Upload Body Photo".
Client-Side (Initial Render): When the JavaScript loads, loadStateFromLS might immediately find a value for LS_BODY_IMAGE_FOR_CANVAS_KEY in localStorage. If it does, bodyImageForCanvas becomes non-null. This causes React to render "Change Body Photo".
This discrepancy between the server-rendered HTML and the initial client-rendered HTML causes the hydration error.

The Fix: To resolve this, we must ensure the initial client render matches the server render. We'll defer loading values from localStorage until after the component has mounted and hydrated, using a useEffect hook.

I will modify src/app/try-on/page.tsx to:

Initialize all states that depend on localStorage with their server-side default values directly in useState.
Create a useEffect hook that runs once after the component mounts (client-side only) to load the actual values from localStorage using loadStateFromLS and then update the states.
This ensures the first render on the client matches the server, preventing the hydration error. Subsequent updates from localStorage will then trigger re-renders as needed.

To further enhance organizational capabilities and editing efficiency, the next logical step is to implement Object Grouping and Ungrouping.

Reasoning:

Enhanced Workflow & Organization: Users often create complex designs from multiple smaller elements. Grouping allows these elements to be treated as a single unit for transformations (moving, scaling, rotating), styling, and layer management. This is essential for intricate tattoo designs.
Alignment with Professional Editors: This is a standard, expected feature in tools like Canva, Illustrator, Photoshop, and GIMP. Its absence makes our editor feel incomplete.
Builds on Existing Features:

Transformations & Properties: Once grouped, transformations and (potentially in the future) some shared properties can be applied to the group.
Foundation for Future Enhancements: Grouping is a prerequisite for features like creating reusable components, symbols, or applying complex effects to a collection of objects.

I'll modify src/app/design-studio/page.tsx to introduce grouping and ungrouping:

New Actions in TopBar:

onGroup: A new function to be passed to TopBar. Enabled when selectedObjects.length > 1.
onUngroup: A new function to be passed to TopBar. Enabled when selectedObjects.length === 1 and the selected object is a fabric.Group.
New props canGroup and canUngroup will control the enabled state of these menu items.
Grouping Logic (within CanvasArea):

handleGroupObjects():
Checks if fabricCanvas and selectedObjects.length > 1.
Creates a new fabric.Group(fabricCanvas.getActiveObjects(), { ... }).
Assigns a unique ID (e.g., Date.now().toString(36) + ...) and a layerName (e.g., "Group") to the new group object.
Removes the original selected objects from the canvas (Fabric.js does this implicitly when creating a group from an active selection, but we'll ensure it).
Adds the new group to the canvas.
Sets the new group as the active object (fabricCanvas.setActiveObject(group)).
Clears the selectedObjects store state and then re-populates it with the new group.
Saves to history.
Ungrouping Logic (within CanvasArea):

handleUngroupObjects():
Checks if fabricCanvas and selectedObjects.length === 1 and selectedObjects[0] instanceof fabric.Group.
Gets the active group: const group = fabricCanvas.getActiveObject() as fabric.Group;
Uses group.toActiveSelection(); which deconstructs the group and creates an active selection of its former child objects.
Calls group.destroy(); to remove the group object itself from the canvas.
The items are now selected as part of an ActiveSelection. The selection:created or selection:updated event on the canvas should update the selectedObjects store state.
fabricCanvas.requestRenderAll();
Saves to history.
Layers Panel Integration:

A fabric.Group will naturally appear as a single object in the layers panel due to fabricCanvas.getObjects().
The existing logic for displaying layerName, type icon (we'll need a generic "group" icon or reuse LayersIcon), visibility, and selection highlighting will work. Object ordering will apply to the group as a whole.
History Management:

Both grouping and ungrouping operations will be added to the undo/redo history stack by saving the canvas JSON state.
This set of changes will make the Design Studio significantly more powerful for managing complex arrangements of objects.
